And all Jews need to understand that this is their moment to take a back seat, not only for their beliefs, but even for their physical safety, for the greater good.

And that’s sort of a very paralyzing position to be in, because there is a greater good. But why are Jews the ones who are being asked to say, Your safety, your beliefs, your history—those have to be secondary to everyone else’s safety?

Nessel: Yeah, let me bring up something that is really fresh in my mind, because it just happened over the course of the weekend. Abdul brought Hasan Piker, the streamer, to our state. For old people like me, I had no idea who this guy was. But he brought him to a number of different universities, and he really helped to elevate his profile in this state. And of course, it’s in all my algorithms now, the things that he says. But one of the things that he did over the course of the weekend, or at least came to my attention over the course of the weekend. He made some statements:



Piker:  Because people don’t [expletive] with Israel any longer. And if, and if Jews in America keep putting, this, this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone’s gonna come around and take action. Not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews.

Nessel: And during the course of it, they actually flashed on the screen, a guy by the name of Jeremy Moss, who was a longtime state legislator in Michigan. He won the Democratic nomination to replace Haley Stevens in the Eleventh Congressional District, an overwhelmingly Democratic district. He’s very likely to be the next congressman from the Eleventh Congressional District to serve in Washington. And he put up a picture of him. He’s Jewish, and he is supportive, generally speaking, of Israel. And next to the picture it had his AIPAC rating, which is this group that puts out, like, any time a Jewish person contributes, basically, to a candidate, that’s AIPAC money.

And next to it, it had a picture of him in Israel surrounded by a number of Israeli flags. It did not say what he was doing there. He was actually there to protest against the Netanyahu government. That wasn’t covered in there. But I thought to myself, Why is Hasan Piker, who has millions and millions of followers—many of us believe that he is very anti-Semitic, in addition to being racist and sexist and many other things, if you listen to some of the things that he says during his streaming or podcast. And I’m wondering, who’s going to stand up for Jeremy when these really hateful words are being said, and you’re highlighting this Jewish elected who’s going to Congress? Who are the members of Congress, of our congressional delegation in Michigan who will say, That’s not right? Who of our U.S. senators, who in our state legislature will do it? Is it only going to be the Jewish electeds? Will it be the same people over and over again, which is me and two state reps and just members of the Michigan Democratic Party Jewish caucus? Is it only going to be a handful of us? Will we have any allies that are non-Jews who will stand up and say, This is wrong?

And so for a lot of us, you know, we feel really isolated. Like, do we have a home in the Democratic Party anymore?

And I actually put up a query on, it was not my political, but my personal Facebook page. So all the people who can see it are people who I’ve friended on there. They’re not just bots, or just people from other states or whatever. These are all people that I know in some way, shape, or another. And I said, Is there still room in the Democratic Party for people who believe that Israel has a right to exist, and that we should have a two-state solution with sovereignty and dignity and self-determination for both the Palestinians and Israeli Jews? And it was a real mixed result. It was half and half, of a lot of people saying, No, our tent of our party is not big enough for you people anymore. And that was deeply concerning for me.

Frum: You mentioned earlier on that you—and this I’m sure is true for everyone who’s ever run for office—have said things that on second thought were not the right thing to say, or showed imperfect understanding or lack of sympathy. And this is part of the human experience, right?

If you’re a candidate who has built all of his or her previous career in a farm area, and then you run for statewide office and you say something that shows lack of awareness of the problems of city dwellers. Or vice versa: You’re a city candidate, and you haven’t been attentive enough to the needs of farmers or rural people, and they come to you and say, Look, you’ve been rural [or] you’ve been urban through the first part of your career, and now you’re running statewide, and you need to understand us. It’s credible that that person said, Gee, I never thought about it that way. I never had to think about city or country, where I was before. You’re right. I’m learning from you. Thank you so much. I can be a bigger and better representative of more people as I run for statewide office.

But if you’ve based your entire career on I hate the farmers, or I hate the city people, and that’s your message, and everything that you don’t like is a product of a conspiracy by farmers or city people, and then you run for statewide office, and we’re a few weeks from a close election and you suddenly realize, I need 100,000 more votes from the farmers—and then every liberal op-ed writer in America is saying, Here’s what you must say to deceive the farmers into thinking you’re their friend in these last few weeks before the election, I think the farmers or the city people are entitled to be a little skeptical. And to say, You know, that’s just a form of words. Your whole career was based on one view. I think that’s you. I think that’s you. The thing you’ve said all your career, I think that’s you. And I don’t think that’s ignorance. I think that’s you. And if I find it disrespectful of me, that’s not because you don’t understand me. It’s because you’ve taken a view hostile to me.

Nessel: I understand exactly what you’re saying. And I want to believe that that Abdul will educate himself a little bit more on some of these issues that I think he demonstrates a clear lack of understanding in regard to, and does not appreciate some of the nuances in the history of Israel or the background of the Jewish people going back 3,000 years. I hope he will do that.

But what I will say about how I’m looking at this election in many ways is—when you talk about the future of Israel, when you talk about the future of the Jewish diaspora, I don’t know if any of it matters if we have no regulations of any kind on AI, and we end up in a situation where literally, I mean, you just saw over the weekend they had the robot competition in China. If you have literally armies of robots that are driven by AI that are able to—and I don’t mean to sound too crazy here—but, like, enslave the human race, I don’t think that’s the craziest idea out there. And I’ve actually heard a lot of these AI CEOs talk about that. They’ve talked about how AI could result in the end of humanity.

Climate change. I mean, every day we are seeing the devastation that’s brought upon us. I don’t know how much longer the human race is going to be able to continue if we don’t take serious measures to combat climate change.

So there are things that I look at when I think, Well, can I support Abdul and, and perhaps other candidates that are like-minded. We’re not going to have to worry about the future of the Israelis and the Palestinians, because I don’t know that any of us are going to continue to exist if we don’t really get these significant global issues under control. I will tell you right now, in Michigan, we’re getting absolutely hammered by these Canadian tariffs. So you have, you know, you have people all—

Frum: By the anti-Canadian tariffs.

Nessel: The anti-Canadian tariffs. Sorry.

Frum: I’m thinking about Canada. I’m on the north shore of Lake Ontario right now. (Laughs.)

Nessel: Okay. So the impact that this is having to us can’t possibly be overstated. I mean, you have people who are going to lose everything, everything, everything, right? They’ll lose their businesses, they’ll lose their homes, they’ll lose their health insurance. So these are real issues that I know that Mike Rogers is going to be terrible on, and will do anything that supports the president no matter how ridiculous his foreign policy may be in a way that is so detrimental to us in Michigan. And I think that Abdul is going to stand up to that.

So there are so many issues. I could go on and on and on. Like, yes; my Judaism is so fundamental to who I am, and what my beliefs are. But what do we do with these crises that are of such enormity that, could it eclipse those other concerns, because they are of such a weighty nature? And that’s going to have to be considerations for me. And I would say to my fellow Michigan Jews who are members of the Democratic Party, or who typically vote for Democrats, these should also be considerations for you. We shouldn’t just be thinking about Israel or even the safety of American Jews when we have all of these other issues that are also incredibly important.

Frum: Well, you, you’re raising a paradox that you will recognize as one of the most foundational questions in Jewish ethics. This quote from the Rabbi Hillel, where he says, “If I’m only for myself, what am I? If I’m not for myself, who am I?” And the subtlety of the quote is obviously—if you’re only for yourself, you’re not even a person, because that’s the what. But if you’re not for yourself, then who are you?

And this is a thing that, in this cycle, a lot of Jews are having to balance. Which is: Most Jews are probably on the side of most of the issues that are represented by the anti-Trump coalition. But important parts of that anti-Trump coalition are saying, But the price of the coalition and of your membership is you must take a second seat, not only for your beliefs about the state of Israel, but even for your physical safety.

So I’m going to ask you to put yourself in—and you are a very highly engaged person; you’re passionately committed to your views—but you must have relatives or friends who are less engaged and who are committed to Jewish survival and to the Jewish connection with the state of Israel. How would you help them to think through the Who am I, what am I question? How, when they’re told this is the right thing to do, but you’re going to have to take a second place in this right thing to do. How should they think about that?

Nessel: This is a daily conversation with my own family, right? I mean, my family that, if you’re talking about my family, without our many cousins and, and whatnot, I mean, probably never voted for a Republican in a U.S. Senate race, ever. Ever! And my parents are 85 and 89 years old, and we’re having these conversations right now.

But I would say a few things. First of all, again, we can’t pretend that this is the only issue facing us, and sometimes we do have to come to the conclusion that we have to do what is best for all of humanity over, you know, those of us obviously who are Jewish, and again, who believe in the right for Israel to exist.

But I want to make this one last point, while I still have the opportunity to do so. I think it’s a fundamental mistake for the Democratic Party to think that you can just push Jewish Democrats out and simply replace them with any other population, you know? We have been such an instrumental part of this party. Whether you’re talking about our activism, whether you’re talking about our legal work, whether you’re talking about the contributions and donations that have been made to the Democratic Party. And the fact that we have very progressive ideals that we’ve worked hard on. And whether you’re looking all the way back—to whether it’s women’s suffrage, whether it’s the fight for rights for African Americans in this country, whether it’s work that I did and many other Jews on LGBTQ-rights issues—we have been an essential part of the fabric of the Democratic Party for a very, very long time. We are an essential part of the fabric of this party, and I would ask the leadership and members of this party to consider that before they do or say things that will force us to leave this party.

I feel like we’re already not wanted in the Republican Party, and I think that this is, you know, essentially a party of fascism. And we know about all the excuses that they make on the far right, and how they embrace the Nick Fuentes and Candace Owens and all the people, and Tucker Carlsons, all of the enormous anti-Semites on the far right.

And I’m not a member of the Republican Party. I can only speak to being a member of the Democratic Party. But I would tell members of our party that this is a worse place without Jews in it.

David Frum: Well, one of the things that people will say, and I think this is a message that Abdul El-Sayed and many of his supporters say, is: All you have to do to be accepted as a Jew is to jettison Israel. That’s all we ask. And just disavow the fate of half the Jewish people who live in the state of Israel. Maybe they’ll be massacred, maybe they’ll be enslaved. Who knows what, maybe they’ll be raped. Just separate yourself from that, and you’ll be left alone.

And I think I listen to that, and I hear, first—it’s not for you to say what is important to me. When you tell me that Israel is not integral to being a Jew, you know, I don’t walk into your house and tell you what is integral to being who you are. So don’t walk into my house and tell me what is integral to being me. But second, that’s a pretty contemptible offer. You’ll guarantee my physical safety if I submit? I mean, 3,000 years of Jewish martyrdom has been people who—it’s a stubborn people, as it says in the Bible itself. We don’t submit to that. And now you’re asking us to, with a threat, maybe sometimes with a smile and a threat, but a threat. Disavow yourself, and you’ll be safe. You say, you know what? The whole point of the state of Israel was that Jews didn’t have to put their safety at the mercy of other people. They could defend themselves. And that’s the Jewish project—is to have a place in the world where Jews are safe because of themselves.

And the American project was to say everyone is safe. It doesn’t matter who you are, because we don’t have majorities that tolerate minorities here. It’s not with permission from other people. It’s not conditional. Your safety is nonconditional. That’s George Washington’s famous letter to the Newport Synagogue. Your safety is nonconditional. You’re an American. You have a right to be the same as anybody else, and to be left alone and respected the same as anybody else. And now suddenly there are all kinds of conditions, but only if you disavow who you are.

Nessel: Yeah. Let me just respond to that in a couple different ways. I’ve said this over and over again, that when a Black person says, That phrase that you’re using, or the way you’re talking about this issue, to me, is racist. I’d like you to stop doing it—we respect that. When we’re talking to somebody in the LGBTQ community and say, I don’t like the phrase that you’re using, or, That term is offensive to me, and here’s why—we respect that in the Democratic Party. We say, Okay, I’m not going to use that phrase anymore. I didn’t realize that it was offensive to you. I’m going to stop. But this has been an outlier for me. I have people saying, You are not going to tell us what you deem to be anti-Semitic. We’ll decide what’s anti-Semitic. That’s not up for you, the Jewish population, to decide. And I find that to be very off-putting and offensive. And I think that’s totally unacceptable.

But the last thing I will say is this, if that’s the deal that has to be made—and I’ve been really candid about this—I was Jewish before I was ever Michigan attorney general. I’m going to be Jewish afterwards. I was Jewish before I was ever a member of the Democratic Party, and if I have to, I’ll be Jewish afterwards, too.

Frum: Attorney General Nessel, thank you so much for joining me today on The David Frum Show.

Nessel: Thanks for having me.

[Music]

Frum: Thanks so much to Dana Nessel for joining me today on The David Frum Show. As mentioned at the top of the program, my book this week is a new biography of Roy Cohn: American Scoundrel: Roy Cohn’s Dark Journey from Joe McCarthy to Donald Trump by Kai Bird and Susan Goldmark.

I had the opportunity to meet the notorious Roy Cohn once in my life, when I was an undergraduate at Yale. He came to address a group of students. It was a small group, because the name of Joe McCarthy’s famous henchman had obscured a little bit with the passage of time. There were maybe six or eight of us there, and we all observed he was just as creepy in person as he was creepy in legend. And that’s the story that is told by Kai Bird and Susan Goldmark in their new book.

Roy Cohn, of course, was the chief aide to Joe McCarthy during his investigations of the early 1950s. Those investigations led to disaster for McCarthy, who was eventually censured by the Senate and who died of alcoholism as a comparatively young man in 1957. But Roy Cohn went on to a more lucrative future, even if he never lost his notoriety.

As a shady lawyer in New York, he handled divorces. He represented many Mafia figures. He was involved in all kinds of proceedings that would have got anybody else disbarred or even sent to prison. But Roy Cohn went from fame to fame, progress to progress. He never paid his taxes. So despite all of his amazing career success, he died broke because he owed millions of dollars to the IRS, which they reclaimed from his estate, leaving very little behind. But he certainly lived life the way he wanted to live it.

Kai Bird and Susan Goldmark tell a withering story of his career, but they also illustrate how many people who thought they despised him and despised his politics were drawn into his orbit because of Roy Cohn’s fathomless ability to find favors that people wanted and to deliver them. He lived by a code of loyalty, and he drew into his network of favor-exchange many people who would become pillars of the New York liberal establishment of the 1960s and 1970s.

Roy Cohn was a bad man, and he fully deserves the nickname of “American scoundrel” that he’s given in this book. But there is a blind spot in the book, and a blind spot in the way that people think about him that I kept dealing with as I read this otherwise fascinating and important book. One of the characteristics of post-McCarthy America is that, having felt so bad about the way people were accused falsely and dragged into conspiracies and had their names besmirched—some of them innocent, some of them merely naive fellow travelers. Some comparatively few of them actual traitors or spies. But there became a kind of blind spot about the moral decision to have been a communist in the 1930s and 1940s, and I noticed that throughout the biography of Roy Cohn.

Kai Bird previously wrote a biography of the great scientist Robert Oppenheimer. In fact, it is his 2005 biography of Robert Oppenheimer that became the basis for the Christopher Nolan 2023 movie. Now, if you’ve seen Oppenheimer, one of the things you see is that Oppenheimer is the victim of a false persecution because of his left-wing sympathies in the 1930s, which are suggested in the movie to amount to no more than a sympathy for the Spanish Republic and a desire and a willingness to make donations to Spanish Republican causes. Many, many, many people of liberal view shared that outlook.

But in the years since 2005, more and more evidence has come to light that, in fact, Oppenheimer was probably a [Communist] party member between 1939 and 1941. That’s the period of the Hitler-Stalin Pact, so this is not a premature anti-fascism. This is not a desire to support the only people who seem to be fighting against Hitler. He joined the party and stayed in it after Stalin signed his pact with Hitler and into the 1941, at least according to the latest suggestive evidence collected post-2005.

One of the most eminent historians of the Cold War period and the atomic-research program, Barton Bernstein wrote on the eve of the release of the Oppenheimer movie, “New evidence also leads to a reassessment and thus taking far more seriously, much negative evidence on Oppenheimer dating back to the 1940s that many historians, including myself, often unwisely in about the 1970s to 2002 period, minimized or disregarded. It is no longer possible or reasonable to comfortably conclude, as had many liberal interpreters, including myself, that Oppenheimer in the 1954 hearing”—that’s his security hearing—“was candidly forthcoming about his late 1930s and early 1940s politics. He was not. He lied, and he sought to deceive.” Now, that story about Oppenheimer is relevant to reading this new book about Roy Cohn.

Again, in this otherwise encyclopedic and analytic biography of Roy Cohn, you see a minimization of what happened in the 1930s and ’40s with actual Communists. In pages 32 and 33 of American Scoundrel, Kai Bird and Susan Goldmark call Whittaker Chambers a serial fabulist and treat it as an open question whether Alger Hiss was indeed guilty of perjury, and that’s not an open question. We know that not only from the investigations that were taken, conducted at the time, but from later releases of Soviet transcripts that identify Alger Hiss as a Soviet asset in the 1930s.

That doesn’t excuse Roy Cohn, who was a scoundrel and who lied and who abused his office and was guilty of, again, things that would get anybody else disbarred or sent to prison. But it does mean that when we reckon with the past, we need to understand that even when we identify the villains correctly, we’re often at risk of identifying the heroes wrongly. Those who are on the wrong side of Roy Cohn were not heroes, even if Roy Cohn was indeed the American scoundrel and great villain that Bird and Goldmark so vividly portray.

That’s it for this week’s David Frum Show. Thank you so much for joining me today. I hope if you like the show that you’ll continue subscribing to The Atlantic. That’s the best way to support the work of me and all of my colleagues. Please share this material on any social-media platform you have access to. That helps with the show’s algorithm. See you next week on The David Frum Show. Bye-bye.

entries.title: The Most Beautiful Woman
entries.summary: What Dolly Parton meant to the South
entries.content:
Growing up in Tennessee, I could hardly walk into a grocery store without hearing “Jolene” playing on the radio. My mom sang fragments of “9 to 5” as she cooked Hamburger Helper on school nights, after clocking out of work. At my babysitter’s house in the summer, where Country Music Television was our ambient noise, she’d shout, “Good golly, Miss Dolly!” every time a Dolly song came on (which was at least every 30 minutes). Dolly Parton was more of an institution than a star to Tennesseans. Her image was plastered on T-shirts and hung on walls, like Mother Mary would be in a Catholic home. We vacationed at her amusement park, Dollywood, every school break. No one ever used her last name—she was simply Dolly to us all, and she was living proof that tough odds were no match for a cup of ambition.

When Dolly’s death was announced yesterday afternoon, my phone lit up with texts from hometown friends. “It feels like a member of our family died in Tennessee today,” one friend said. My socialist sister said Tennessee’s poet laureate had left us. My Donald Trump–voting father cried. In Tennessee, whether you fly a MAGA flag or a Pride flag, one thing is for sure: You’re listening to Dolly.

Dolly mattered to southerners for so many reasons, but perhaps most of all for her origin story, which she called a “rags to rhinestones” tale. She grew up four hours east of me, in a one-room cabin with her 11 siblings, in the depths of Tennessee Appalachia. Unlike Nashville, which is so associated with Dolly today, the Appalachian region of Tennessee is riddled with evidence of isolation in its language, economy, and general sense of yearning. Appalachia has its own distinct dialect and a deep tradition of oral storytelling. Being able to captivate an audience served as capital, and she brought this generationally reinforced skill to songwriting and the stage.

Her upbringing was one of poverty and stripped-down performance. Like many other Tennessee families, the Parton family sang church hymns and mountain ballads on front-porch swings. In her hit song “Coat of Many Colors,” Dolly recalls a coat her mother made for her of donated scrap fabric. “Although we had no money, I was rich as I could be / In my coat of many colors my mama made for me.” She was proud of and honest about her roots, and for many poor southerners, it was the first time they saw their stories told publicly.

Dolly was first introduced on the Grand Ole Opry stage at age 13 by Johnny Cash, who called her “a little girl here from up in East Tennessee.” She would never shed that identity. A number of global superstars got their start in the South, including Taylor Swift and Dolly’s own goddaughter, Miley Cyrus. Most ditched their southern dialect and opted for a more conventional pop sound after reaching the height of their fame. But Dolly never evolved. Her famous mantra, “Find out who you are and do it on purpose,” explained the way she viewed the world. She was unapologetically southern, and at the same time, nobody’s fool. “Dolly’s accent, like her music, held the notes of her East Tennessee home, and she often spoke proudly of her choice to carry it,” Amy Clark, a linguist from Appalachia, told me. “She sounded just like many of us in the way she said ‘light’ or dropped ‘g’ off certain words.” Her refusal to abandon her southern way of speaking meant the world to people from such places. “If you were from Appalachia and couldn’t carry a note, you could still be proud because you sounded like Dolly,” Clark said.

Many stars who have left (or, in their view, escaped) the South speak of their upbringing as a past life rarely revisited. Dolly, conversely, spent her entire life giving back to her home state. “She understood that where you come from isn’t something you transcend,” Brooke Griffith, a jewelry-shop owner from East Tennessee, wrote on Instagram. “It’s something you can honor by creating opportunities for the people who come after you.” And Dolly did just that, most famously by opening Dollywood in 1986. It’s the largest employer in Sevier County, where she grew up. After Whitney Houston popularized her song “I Will Always Love You,” Dolly invested the royalties she earned into a big office complex and strip mall in a predominantly Black Nashville neighborhood. She called it “the house that Whitney built,” and mentioned it only when asked about it.

When Dolly’s identity didn’t match the plans pop culture had for her, she chose her roots, and was rewarded every time. Even her look was defiantly southern. A 1991 issue of Vanity Fair described Dolly as “every down-home virtue wrapped up in a sizzling blonde bombshell.” That’s the thing that drew me to Dolly all those years ago—she seemed to be the only woman in the South who could present as so sexy and be read as so wholesome. Most women who wore Daisy Dukes were whispered about in church pews and grocery lines, but Dolly wasn’t just loved in spite of it; she was lauded for it. Her self-described “Backwoods Barbie” persona, also the name of one of her songs, inspired generations of women who might be cast out as trailer trash to lean into their interpretation of beauty. “So read into it what you will, but see me as I am / The way I look is just a country girl’s idea of glam,” the song goes.

She drew her aesthetic inspiration from a woman she’d seen as a kid when her family went into town. “There was this woman that was the town-trash whore, they called her, but I thought she was beautiful,” Dolly told Ellen DeGeneres once. She described the woman’s look in a way that many would describe Dolly’s—blond hair piled on her head, red nails, tall heels. “I just thought she was the prettiest thing I’d ever seen. And I used to say to my mama, ‘Oh, she’s so pretty.’ Mama’d say, ‘Oh, she’s just trash.’ And I thought to myself, That’s what I want to be when I grow up—just trash!” she said. “Most country girls—that’s the way you think you’re supposed to look, as plain as we were. We had nothing.”

I remember finding that exact same kind of woman the most beautiful. To be buxom and blond with a well-painted face was many southern girls’ dream, and we saw it embodied in Dolly, who never apologized for her presentation. She paired pageant glam with a Walmart push-up bra. She was equal parts Bible verses and witty comebacks. She was whiskey in a teacup, and to a little Southern Baptist with an affinity for lipstick and boundary-pushing, she was proof that one could love both God and dime-store glamour.

Dolly showed us southern girls that you didn’t have to sacrifice femininity to be taken seriously. In my own life, she’s empowered me to keep my humor and silliness, even in spaces where that’s not the norm. She taught a generation of young southern women that there’s nothing more powerful than to be underestimated; you should never correct someone who thinks you’re dumb, because that just means they’ll see you as harmless and let you into any room. And that’s when you get to kindly prove them wrong. No one better embodied the warmth and sheer grit of a southern woman.

To be a female country artist who reached the heights that Dolly did was not only rare but absolutely unprecedented. Dolly made sure to bring classic country music to new audiences. She was the ultimate collaborator. With more than 100 collaborations throughout her career, she partnered with the giants of other genres, including Paul McCartney, Pitbull, Beyoncé, Norah Jones, Post Malone, and Sabrina Carpenter. Her two Trio albums with Linda Ronstadt and Emmylou Harris showed what could happen when three titans of the country, Americana, and rock industries combined forces. She always kept her country Dolly flair no matter the style of the collaboration. This helped new audiences recognize the beauty in traditional country music, while introducing her older fan base to other genres previously foreign to them. So much of the country-music craze we see today can be attributed to Dolly’s presence across different types of music.

But Dolly’s influence went well beyond representation in the media; Dolly’s Imagination Library has changed the lives of millions of young children, including my own two nieces. Founded in 1995 with her father, who was illiterate, the program provides free books to kids from birth to age 5, regardless of their income. Participants in pre-K also receive a free year pass to Dollywood, which my youngest niece used just last month when we visited. Today the organization gives millions of books monthly to children around the world.

My best friend from high school was a lower-income kid who, like so many others, was introduced to reading by the Imagination Library. Her mother got pregnant with her when she was 22. She was enrolled in a federal food-aid program and remembers splitting kids’ meals at McDonald’s with her daughter in her daughter’s early years. “I didn’t have my shit together when I had her,” she told me. “But my baby got a book once a month until she went to kindergarten. Even though books weren’t something I could afford, I got to read to her.” She compared Dolly’s passing to the day she found out Princess Diana had died.

No southerner, or perhaps human, has remained so universally beloved for so long. In a March poll of Americans’ opinions about international figures, Dolly ranked No. 1 by a long shot, with her two nearest contenders, Barack Obama and Volodymyr Zelensky, falling behind her by more than 50 percentage points. Only 5 percent of the Americans polled said they had an unfavorable opinion of Dolly.

Her universal likability, particularly in the South, could be attributed to all sorts of factors. Maybe it was because, once she did make it big, she paid it forward and gave back to the communities that had built her up. Maybe it was because she avoided talking politics, so everyone could assume she was secretly on their side (she did, however, stand openly with the LGBTQ community, and she created overtly feminist music). Maybe it was because she grew up poor with no connections and made it anyway, embodying an American dream that so many of us have given up on. Our ubiquitous love for Dolly is proof that we still want to root for that dream, especially in a place like Tennessee.

When I walked into Dollywood with my nieces for their first time last month, I got to watch two little Tennesseans fall in love with Dolly the way I did around their age. But she was no stranger to them—they were already good friends by that point. She had sent them books and special birthday messages since they were babies, she had given my youngest niece a ticket to the park, and both girls had read all about her life. “Dolly loves butterflies—that’s why they’re everywhere,” my 7-year-old niece informed me as we walked past the choo choo train. “She’s just so fancy,” my 5-year-old niece declared as we admired her old dresses. For two girls from a Tennessee town with a poverty rate twice that of the national one, Dolly serves as a beacon of what’s possible.

We didn’t know then that it’d be the last time we’d see the place when it wasn’t a memorial—and what an absurdly magical place it is. Who else could get away with naming an entire amusement park after themselves while they’re still alive? Only a saint like Dolly. God rest her soul.

Illustration sources: Andrew Putler / Redferns / Getty; olhahladiy / Getty; MirageC / Getty.

entries.title: The Real Reason Trump Wants Economic Sanctions in Iran
entries.summary: The quieter, longer-term strategy could help push the conflict out of the minds of voters ahead of the midterms.
entries.content:
The quieter, longer-term strategy could help push the conflict out of the minds of voters ahead of the midterms.

Updated at 1:40 p.m. ET on August 26, 2026.

For months, President Trump has been unable to bring the conflict with Iran to a close. A massive bombing campaign lost its effectiveness, and U.S. munitions supplies ran low. Diplomacy lagged, as leaders in Tehran remained content to deliberately prolong the process and harden their control over the Strait of Hormuz. Even the current pseudo-cease-fire—as deeply uneasy as it is—has done little to meaningfully lower the cost of energy around the globe.

With few options remaining, the Trump administration has settled into a potentially lengthy campaign of economic pressure, pledging to squeeze Iran until its leaders have no choice but to seriously return to negotiations. But that tack could prove toothless if the U.S. doesn’t also punish the nations that still do business with Iran and keep its economy afloat—and Trump has historically shown little willingness to stand up to the likes of China and Russia, or even North Korea, which has a strategic alliance with Tehran.

If nothing else, the new approach allows the White House to say it’s trying something and then—importantly—to stop talking about the war. Part of the plan, Trump advisers and allies tell us, is to try to push Iran to the background, while hoping that gas prices come down even a little and that Republicans can shift the nation’s focus to more politically palatable topics ahead of the midterms.

That won’t change the reality on the ground in the Middle East: Alliances have been strained, the U.S. military has been overtaxed, and Iran wields far more power in the region than it did at the beginning of the war, about six months ago. But it could allow Trump, a master of distraction, to turn to other priorities—a trade war with Canada! Claims of election fraud! His skill at flagpoles!—to try to save at least one chamber of Congress for his party this fall.

“We’re just trying to hang on until the midterms,” one Trump adviser told us.

At this moment, strategists in both parties believe that the Democrats are favored to capture the House. And despite a GOP-friendly Senate map, the upper chamber is viewed as a toss-up. Trends were already working against Republicans: Traditionally, the party out of power tends to do well in the midterms, and over the past decade, Trump supporters have seemed less inclined to vote when his name isn’t on the ballot. The president hasn’t done much to help, and his poll numbers have plunged, even on the economy and immigration, his usual strengths. Republicans, fearing hostility, have largely opted to forgo town halls this summer, skipping what tends to be an effective way to reach constituents. A few of those who have held gatherings in their districts have faced anger and tough questions about Iran, including why the U.S. launched the war in the first place.

Republicans have been urging the White House to wrap up the conflict and reduce its drag on the nation’s economy—and their reelection chances. But a solution has proved elusive. Trump’s goals for the conflict were never well enunciated and have shifted many times. Gone are lofty promises about regime change or preventing Iran from having a nuclear program. Instead, the president has privately told his political allies that once the Strait of Hormuz is reopened, he is inclined to simply declare victory and move on, one outside adviser and a senior administration official told us on the condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations. But even that has proved vexing: Iran has continued to menace ships traveling through the strait and has insisted upon charging a fee or toll. Other countries in the region have declared that unacceptable—the strait was, after all, open and free before the war—though Trump has waffled on whether or not he could live with it. The president said yesterday that the last of the Iranian mines had been removed from the channel, but an official from a country in the region stressed to us that even if that were to remain true, Iran could still terrorize ships with small boats, handheld rocket launchers, and drones.

Republicans have signaled to the White House their approval of its new economic pressure campaign, which was announced by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent earlier this week. The White House’s political shop hopes the plan creates a quiet stranglehold—Bessent deemed it “economic asphyxiation”—that could make steady progress in resolving the conflict while having the added bonus of keeping it out of the headlines. (Trump’s bellicose threats toward Iran have unfailingly driven news cycles and hurt Republicans.) Some in the administration believe that emerging divides in Tehran’s leadership could prompt talks. And if the new sanctions did bring Iran to the table before November, then maybe a renewed stab at diplomacy could juice the markets—and provide an 11th-hour boost for Republicans.

Trump has been bored of the war for a while. Aides have been pushing him to focus on the economy to help Republican candidates, but he has continued to downplay the nation’s affordability challenges, much to his aides’ chagrin. And while Trump remains furious at Iran’s unwillingness to bend, aides have persuaded him to give the new plan a chance. In some ways, it’s not an original idea: Trump has relied on an economic “maximum pressure” campaign since his first term to try to force Iran to abandon its nuclear program. But the intelligence community was mistaken in its belief that Iran would buckle quickly under the financial strain. The regime seems willing to endure significant hardship, and its own citizens’ struggles, to maintain its grip on power. And the new approach carries its own political risks. If Iran proves resilient again, the pressure campaign may have to stretch beyond the midterms, leaving prices high in the interim.

White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told us in a statement that the United States has already “destroyed Iran’s military capabilities” and is now “strangling what’s left of its abysmal economy” by severing its remaining financial lifelines. “They will stand alone, broke, and isolated,” Wales wrote. “The President has been clear: he will always advance America’s interests and never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

The U.S. military has not struck Iran in weeks. This month’s relative reprieve follows a long pattern of using force to try to extract concessions from Iran and failing. After a 13-day strike campaign in July, the U.S. military privately assessed that extending the campaign would lead to diminishing returns—and worsen the nation’s extraordinary munitions shortage.

Earlier this month, Steve Feinberg, the No. 2 leader at the Pentagon, sent a memo demanding that the defense industry rapidly expand its production. Over the course of the war, the U.S. has used many of its Tomahawks, drones, and air-defense munitions. A July 27 assessment by the Center for Strategic and International Studies concluded that the war has significantly depleted U.S. air-defense stocks—particularly of Patriot and THAAD interceptors—and that replenishing those munitions to prewar levels would take years. Last week, Raytheon announced it had been awarded a $22.9 billion contract that would “dramatically accelerate the production of Tomahawk cruise missiles.” Still, the administration insists its stockpile is robust.

There have been other costs to the American military: Eighteen service members have been killed, and bases in the region have been damaged. The USS Abraham Lincoln’s 5,000 sailors and Marines spent more than 270 consecutive days at sea without a port visit; the carrier’s extended deployment was marked by reports of food and supply shortages, plumbing problems, and declining morale. Only in recent days did it leave the region, bound for Asia, though the U.S. is keeping two aircraft-carrier strike groups nearby—the USS George Washington and the USS George H. W. Bush.

Iran has also largely stopped its strikes toward U.S. bases across the region. Last week, the United Arab Emirates said that Iran had launched two ballistic missiles that splashed down in the Persian Gulf, one within the Emirates’ territorial waters—the last known instance of Iranian aggression (though Tehran denied involvement). On Monday, an oil tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile in the Omani shipping lane through the Strait of Hormuz, damaging its engine room and disabling the vessel. The crew was unharmed, and no one has yet claimed responsibility.

Trump has never been one to show much discipline, and could lose patience with the waiting game. But Iran also gets a say in determining what happens between now and November. More punitive American sanctions are likely to provoke a response from Iran, particularly because its leaders want the U.S. to feel the costs of the war. Iran is also watching the midterm elections closely; some officials fear that Trump could become more aggressive in the weeks after ballots are cast. That could prompt Iran to escalate first—and once more put the war back into voters’ minds.

entries.title: Why Was This Looney Tunes Movie Almost Shelved for Good?
entries.summary: The director of Coyote vs. Acme wants to make sense of the film’s near death.
entries.content:
The director of Coyote vs. Acme wants to make sense of the film’s near death.

Perhaps the starkest sign that Coyote vs. Acme isn’t your typical children’s movie is that it’s based on a New Yorker article. Yes, it features many Looney Tunes characters that multiple generations know and love, interacting alongside real-life actors in a style similar to prior big-screen efforts, such as Space Jam or Looney Tunes: Back in Action. But the director Dave Green’s film—which opens August 28, after a protracted saga that almost saw it kept from audiences forever—draws from a slyly funny “Shouts & Murmurs” story from 1990. Written by the humorist Ian Frazier, “Coyote v. Acme” has a wry and self-aware premise: What would happen if Wile E. Coyote, the Looney Tune on a constantly unsuccessful hunt for the ever-chipper Road Runner, filed a lawsuit against the (fictional) Acme Corporation for selling him faulty products?

“I thought the baseline idea for the movie was just, like, the funniest thing in the world,” Green told me in a recent interview, reminiscing about when he first signed on to direct the film, back in 2019. He wasn’t the first person in the film industry to be charmed by Frazier’s story. Despite the erudite tone, the simple notion of Wile E. Coyote pursuing legal action was amusing enough to Hollywood producers that various attempts were made to develop it for the screen, dating back to an effort by the producer Scott Rudin in the late 1990s.

Warner Bros., which owns Looney Tunes, jump-started the latest version of the project in 2018, and Green completed it in 2022. Coyote vs. Acme was initially scheduled to debut the following summer, but it was taken off the schedule early into production; a new release date was never announced. In the fall of 2023, Warner Bros. told the director that the movie would be shelved entirely. The studio reportedly made the call for a tax write-off—the latest in a series of such decisions, as it dealt with debt issues after the coronavirus pandemic.

Three years later, Coyote vs. Acme is finally entering theaters. After years of limbo, it ended up in the hands of Ketchup Entertainment, an independent distributor that has now become its unlikely savior. The company cut a $50 million deal with Warner Bros. for it last March. “I continued to not believe it, up until now, when I still can’t believe it,” Green said. “It’s a completely surreal reality to check into. But it seems to be happening—I think it’s happening,” he added with a laugh.

His trepidation is understandable: The path the film took to cinemas reflects Hollywood’s continued post-pandemic instability, even as theatergoing has picked back up. Coyote vs. Acme had reportedly tested well with audiences and featured some of Warner Bros.’ most well-known creations, yet the cancellation suggests the company still expected to lose too much money on the project.

The wildest part of the production, Green admitted, was how easy it was at first. When asked by Warner Bros. to pitch ideas for an adaptation of Frazier’s article, the director proposed something along the lines of a true-crime documentary crossed with a legal drama. To his surprise, the studio didn’t immediately turn him down. “It almost felt like everything was a ‘yes,’ and there were no boundaries. So then I got really excited,” Green said. “They were looking for a take and they were looking for something that would help them narrow in. And, as different as my tonal comparisons were, I think they responded to the fact that there was a take in it.”

Green’s notion was to take the tropes of underdog courtroom movies—he cited The Insider, Erin Brockovich, and A Few Good Men as inspirations—and place cartoon characters within them. The humans they interact with (played by Will Forte, Lana Condor, and John Cena, among others) would treat Wile E. Coyote’s lawsuit with humdrum seriousness. “That’s the kind of behavior that really comes from Looney Tunes historically,” Green said—winking references to grown-up media that its young audience might not understand. “It’s Bugs Bunny in Casablanca or Elmer Fudd at the opera, poking at high art.” That device has become a hallmark of the franchise, with self-aware comedy making up the bulk of its spin-off Tiny Toon Adventures and of Looney Tunes’ spiritual successor, Animaniacs.

The devious extra twist of Coyote vs. Acme, however, comes from watching the Looney Tunes themselves navigate human society, with its mundane rules and morals. The story is set in Albuquerque, and the live-action sequences were shot almost entirely on location, lending the kind of jarring verisimilitude Green was hoping for—the animated elements pop against the dusty backdrop. Wile E. Coyote is still capable of speaking only through hand gestures and written signs, but he’s hoping to get a personal-injury lawyer named Kevin Avery (Forte) to help him sue Acme; the manufacturing company is presented as a corporate juggernaut that sells products to both humans and cartoons, while gleefully cutting corners in the name of profit.

The result is explosively zany. It’s also surprisingly sensitive—a quality often lacking from the anarchic Looney Tunes. In bite-size animated form, Wile E. Coyote has a monomaniacal obsession with destroying the Road Runner that’s designed to be a recurring, villainous gag; here, it’s a sad compulsion, a habit he cannot kick. The turn works because it doesn’t feel dark, but rather sweetly relatable. “What if you treated Wile E. like a person and his pain as real?” Green asked. “Then that kind of led to the path of, like, what if it’s about cartoon characters being treated unfairly? That kind of split the whole thing open in a fun way.”

Green shot the movie in spring 2022, an experience he describes as entirely pleasant. “There was actually a lot of support from even the very highest-up voices at the studio, and they were really positive in reacting to my initial cut,” he recalled. Yet that summer, Warner Bros. made the surprising decision to shelve Batgirl, a $90 million HBO Max production. “That was really scary to us,” Green said. “But we never thought we were in the same danger.” Batgirl seemed plagued by various other corporate maneuvers: a shift away from movies produced exclusively for streaming, and a general impending reset of the DC Comics cinematic universe. (Analysts also believed that Warner Bros. intended to take a write-down on Batgirl, to help alleviate its multibillion-dollar debt.) Still, the decision alarmed many filmmakers, who now had to worry that studios might choose to just delete their work instead of bothering to release it.

Coyote vs. Acme was initially slated to debut July 21, 2023, before Warner Bros. decided to put Barbie in that summer slot. After that, Green remembered, his cast and crew waited for a rescheduled date, which never came. Finally, in November, the studio told him that Coyote vs. Acme would not be released at all. A public outcry from both fans and members of the industry quickly pressured Warner Bros. to shop the movie to other distributors, including Amazon, Apple, and Netflix. The studio’s price tag, however, was reportedly too high for these potential buyers, and Warner Bros. eventually rejected all competing bids to hand it over—an apparent death sentence for Coyote vs. Acme.

Green recalled a fellow director comforting him during this period by saying, “You got away with it. You robbed the bank. You made a courtroom drama for kids starring Looney Tunes characters. In so many ways, this movie should not exist.” Still, as Green told it, the thinking behind pulling Coyote vs. Acme was never fully clear to him. Although it is more complex than a typical kids’ film, the good test-viewing scores and positive critical reception suggest there’s an audience for it. Ketchup Entertainment can’t afford the large marketing budget that a more established studio could have; it is likely looking to recoup costs through international sales and at-home rentals. That Warner Bros. abandoned all of this goodwill and earnings potential, to Green, was somewhat baffling.

But he feels lucky to have finished the film—which he called an “impossibility” for its blend of classic Looney Tunes absurdity and legal-thriller influences—in the first place. Now it has finally escaped containment; Green, it seems, has successfully rewritten his movie’s real-life ending.

entries.title: The Jason Arday Truthers
entries.summary: The concerted effort to airbrush the late fabulist’s life
entries.content:
In death, Jason Arday has become two people. To many readers of legacy newspapers, the late Cambridge University academic is a proven fabulist. The life story on which he built his career, of being nonverbal until 11 because of autism, and then learning to read at 18 and becoming a professor, has “no precedent in medical literature,” as The New York Times delicately put it. Among many other extraordinary claims, his tale of being menaced by a knife-wielding man at Cambridge could not be corroborated, and neither could the story that his family had received a pig’s head as an act of racist intimidation. “To be honest with you, I thought you’d just believe me,” he told a Guardian reporter who challenged him.

That is one reality. However, another one dominates left-wing new media, activist nonprofits, and visual social networks such as Instagram and TikTok. There, the prevailing narrative is that Arday did nothing seriously wrong and Britain’s right-wing media hounded an exceptional Black scholar to his death on August 14 for no reason except racism. Well-wishers have raised more than $300,000 for his family, and made his upcoming memoir a best seller in Britain. At a rally in central London held in his memory, attendees carried placards reading Rest in Power Professor Jason Arday, even though he had resigned the title days before his death. They wanted to make clear their belief that he was unfairly deprived of his academic status.

For some of Arday’s supporters, acknowledging that any of the media scrutiny was justified has become tantamount to siding with his “killers.” He is instead a martyr—the victim of a “lynching”—and the inconvenient fact of his fabulism must be tidied away from the virtual shrine. This is an emotional position rather than a rational one, and its very indefensibility makes it a greater demonstration of tribal loyalty. Insisting that the academic was completely innocent, in the face of all the evidence, sends a strong social signal that you hate the right-wing media and care about racism.

The central question in this dispute is whether the treatment of Arday—the subject of more than 200 articles in print this year, according to CNN, and hundreds more online—was proportionate. The smaller his alleged offenses, the more easily one can argue that the media hounded him to death. And so Arday has been recast as a small-time plagiarist; academics have lined up to argue that, You know, even that isn’t a very big deal. The “meaning of plagiarism does not cover mere overlap of sentences,” the academic Jason Stanley asserted in a blog post that also bizarrely noted that he hadn’t paid much attention to the story because he had been on vacation in Europe. Stanley’s blithe dismissal will be news to students who are told the exact opposite early in their courses. Or to Ross Barkan, who was dropped from New York magazine after getting caught recycling other writers’ words.

Another popular declaration is that Arday “was cleared of plagiarism” by Liverpool John Moores University, where he received his doctorate. This is technically true. When concerns were raised about his dissertation, Cambridge University declined to investigate, saying it was a problem for Liverpool John Moores, which had already stated that it stood by his work. Just before Arday’s death, however, Cambridge reversed its position, pledging to investigate, as did other institutions that had employed Arday. (Arday then resigned from Cambridge, adding that the move should not be “mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me.”) Stressing that he was “cleared” misses the point; the exact allegation is that universities’ lack of interest in scrutinizing Arday represented a failure of institutional checks. Now anyone can run Arday’s thesis through plagiarism-detection software themselves and make up their own mind. When Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz, a writer who otherwise found the media coverage racist, did so, he concluded that “Arday was definitely guilty.”

Keeping a narrow focus on the doctoral thesis is helpful to the pro-Arday side. He also faced a far more serious charge of academic fraud—that he lifted interviewees’ quotations from a 2016 paper in BMJ Open and inserted them into the mouths of people he had supposedly spoken with in his own research, implying outright fabrication of interviews that never occurred. After Cambridge was made aware of this accusation in 2023 by other academics, the journal Social Sciences took an Arday paper offline and then uploaded it again with the offending quotations excised and other direct quotes edited. (Another paper of his in a different journal was also subsequently corrected.) Arday essentially admitted to the misattribution by agreeing to the amendments, although he had earlier told the researcher who raised the issue that questioning him was “bullying and harassment.”

The postmortem airbrushing of Arday’s story also ignores how that story twisted and turned while he was alive. When The Guardian confronted him with the implausibility of some of his tall tales, Arday responded by editing them in real time: Yes, he had once claimed to have run 600 miles in six days, an exceptional feat for an endurance athlete, but what he actually meant was that he took daylong rest breaks in between. Yes, he had claimed to have raised more than £5 million for charity, but actually this was with the help of “many fundraising collectives” whose participants he could not name because they had signed nondisclosure agreements.

The Arday partisans have seized on the thinnest of straws. Defending his philanthropic record, the Byline Times, a British website that bills itself as offering “what the papers don’t say,” implied that the relevant charities’ huge fundraising capacity made his claims credible. “A Byline Times analysis of the publicly identifiable charities Arday was associated with for two decades found that they had a combined gross income of approximately £1.4 billion to £1.5 billion,” it reported, “putting his £5 million collective fundraising claim at well under 1% of their overall income.” That sensation you can feel is your brain melting out through your ears and trickling down your neck. The same analysis would uphold my claim to have, say, just donated six fighter jets to the U.S. government, because they cost a minuscule fraction of the nearly $1 trillion defense budget. Why would you doubt me?

One of the biggest promoters of the revisionist narrative is the Good Law Project, a nonprofit chiefly known in Britain for its patchy record of challenging legal decisions, and for the unforgettable viral incident in which its founder, Jolyon Maugham, voluntarily confessed to having beaten a fox to death with a baseball bat while wearing his wife’s kimono. The Good Law Project intervened on Arday’s behalf early in the news cycle, describing the initial coverage as a “malicious” witch hunt based on “fake accusations of plagiarism.” It mustered an open letter in his defense.

What followed was a classic Streisand effect: The newspapers defended themselves by seeking further corroboration of Arday’s fabulism. As the allegations mounted, various signatories disappeared from the letter, indicating that they found the evidence concerning. By August 8, Maugham was distancing himself, saying that his decision to “carry—a deliberately neutral verb—an open letter in support of Dr Arday” relied on Cambridge’s judgment. He stated that he had not personally evaluated Arday’s broader trustworthiness. “It is expedient for me to say, but it is also true for me to say, that: I only last night returned from ‘holiday,’” he wrote.

After Arday’s death, though, Maugham also offered a new statement, in which he had in fact been closely involved with the letter, and furthermore had intervened in the hope of dissuading the left-wing Guardian from publishing its own damning exposé of Arday. The stated rationale was that the academic was vulnerable, that the right was already attacking him, and that Arday believed (without offering any evidence) that the Guardian reporter Lanre Bakare had a beef with him.

Some people seem to think this was reasonable—that the subjects of unflattering articles should get to veto their publication. Journalism cannot work this way. Maugham’s failed attempt to spike a story on Arday’s behalf became yet more fodder for the narrative of the evil, racist press versus Jason the Martyr. Never mind that Bakare is himself of African descent, or that, as a note hastily appended to Maugham’s statement acknowledged, Arday had initially approached Bakare with his story about the pig’s head and the marauding knifeman.

The academic had wanted his story in the public domain—but only if the journalist endorsed it. Bakare’s real offense was finding no evidence for Arday’s outlandish claims, and saying so.

Why dwell on this depressing, convoluted saga? Many people will be thinking: The poor guy quit, and now he is dead. First, because Arday’s memoir, Great and Unfortunate Things, is still advertised for sale on Amazon UK with absolutely no mention of the controversy surrounding its wild claims. (Arday’s family wanted to continue with publication.) “That oft-used word ‘inspirational’ feels wholly inadequate to describe his incredible story of grit and resilience,” an endorsement sourced from the industry publication The Bookseller declares.

The word incredible is the correct one: My colleague Dan Engber reported how several of the most eye-catching claims in the book’s proposal were swapped for different, but equally dramatic, claims in the finished text. (Arday’s publisher did not respond to his questions about the changes.) As Engber wrote:

The proposal also lays out many of the same events as the memoir but with slightly different dates and details: The boys who beat him up were not his age but four years older; his suicide attempt happened before, not during, the pandemic. And whereas the book describes Arday as having survived two brain tumors, the proposal says he had a bout of testicular cancer. No reference to that illness appears in the memoir.

Nor does the book describe the time that Arday, then a teenager, was struck by a car and spent several months in a coma.

A second reason that the story still resonates is that Arday’s death—the version of it in which he is a complete innocent, hounded by feral, racist journalists—is now being used for political purposes in Britain. The Good Law Project and its allies have demanded the resignation of Cambridge’s vice-chancellor for failing to support Arday; the defenestration of various journalists who covered the story or edited the newspapers in which it appeared; and a public inquiry into Arday’s death, with the desired outcome being tighter restrictions on what the press can publish. Groups affiliated with Amnesty UK have even endorsed “Arday’s Law,” whereby the number of news articles on any person would be capped. This proposal is nonsensical. Do activists really believe that, if The New York Times has used up the entire press’s monthly Trump-scandal quota, everyone else should fall silent?

The Arday case is endlessly debatable because it contains so many double-edged elements. Yes, the academic—one of relatively few Black professors in Britain—was subject to extra scrutiny because of his race. Equally, though, Arday absolutely traded on his identity and his life story. “In his keynotes, Arday focuses on how his identity as a Black autistic man has shaped his experiences in the academic world,” the blurb on his (since-deleted) profile at the Simon & Schuster Speakers Bureau reads.

Undeniably, many of Arday’s detractors treated him not as a fallible human but as a stand-in for the debate over diversity, equity, and inclusion. The academic whose Substack post kicked off the coverage, Nathan Cofnas, is a “race realist” who reveled in the fact that he had taken down someone he saw as the beneficiary of a corrupt, anti-white system. When I asked Cofnas why he had decided to immolate his career by arguing that Black people are academically inferior to white people, he told me that “wokism is the ideology of taking the equality thesis seriously” and that “the only way to defeat the destructive ideology of wokism is to show that it is based on a false empirical premise.”

A few days before we spoke over email, Cofnas was suspended by Ghent University, in Belgium, where he is a postdoctoral scholar, because of the negative publicity he had generated. This news caused widespread rejoicing on the left: A lot of onlookers who were until that moment very opposed to people losing academic jobs amid media storms suddenly decided that this phenomenon was, in fact, good. (An open letter is currently in circulation defending Cofnas.)

Without question, the media coverage of Arday was harsh and high-volume. But much of that volume came from competing outlets breaking fresh news, as more and more of Arday’s extraordinary claims crumbled under scrutiny. Some commentators have argued that coverage ought to have stopped after his resignation. I feel differently; the reporting should (and I think would) have stopped if he admitted to the fabulism. But Arday died still maintaining that he had never lied, and his memoir is on sale, untroubled by corrections to anecdotes that now seem enormously implausible.

Unfortunately, unlike Arday’s fabrications, anti-Black racism in Britain is only too real. But you can believe in that without believing in Jason Arday.
